draft.author: USP India
draft.body_html:
Two of the village’s oldest basket makers are among them.

Firebrands in spirit and confidence, they bring the same energy and assurance to their craft that comes from years of experience.

They have spent years making baskets, working with materials, patterns and techniques that have long been part of everyday life in the village.

For them, much of it is second nature. They know how to shape a basket, work with the materials and make the small adjustments that come only with experience.

As younger women in Rakhigarhi develop their basket-making skills, these two women are an important source of knowledge and inspiration.

Their traditional forms, colours, patterns, and techniques give the baskets their distinctive character. As new designs and ideas are explored through creative exchange, their work remains an important reference point.

The aim is not to replace what already exists, but to build upon it—retaining the authenticity of the craft while allowing it to find new expression.

What USP hopes to do is help that knowledge remain relevant and create opportunities for another generation.

A craft continues not only because someone knows how to make it, but because someone else learns.

seo.description: Two experienced makers and the knowledge that younger women are learning from and building upon.

draft.standfirst: Years of skill and experience. A source of inspiration for a new generation of basket makers.
draft.title: The OG Basket Makers

draft.author: USP India
draft.body_html:
The haveli does not reveal itself all at once.

As restoration progresses, attention turns to details that might otherwise go unnoticed—carved panels, layers of plaster, decorative screens and traces of earlier repairs. Each offers a glimpse into how the building was made and how it has changed over time.

Understanding what remains is an important part of deciding what to retain, what needs repair and how best to approach the work.

Local workers learn alongside conservation professionals, gaining practical experience with traditional materials and building techniques as the restoration unfolds.

These photographs capture moments in that process. The building is still being studied, repaired and gradually brought back into use.

The work will leave its mark on the haveli. The knowledge gained along the way can extend beyond it.

seo.description: Looking closely at what remains, and at the knowledge developing as the haveli is brought back into use.

draft.author: USP India
draft.body_html:
Going door to door in Rakhigarhi, we asked women if they had anything at home that had been handmade by a mother or grandmother.

The answer was almost always the same:

“No, nothing.”

We continued visiting homes, and a group of curious women began to gather around us.

We began asking differently. Was there something handmade that had been used for years, but was now tucked away because it was no longer needed?

Sometimes there was a pause. Then someone would go home and return with something. Another woman would remember something she had. Soon, things began to appear.

What struck us was that these objects were not regarded as anything particularly remarkable. They had simply been part of everyday life.

But they held knowledge: of local materials, colour, pattern, and how things were made and used.

We had been asking about craft. What we began to see was knowledge that had been there all along.

That changed the conversation.

Instead of asking what might be introduced to Rakhigarhi, we began to look more closely at what was already there—and what might grow from it.

seo.description: Going door to door in Rakhigarhi revealed handmade objects and knowledge that had been quietly kept all along.

draft.standfirst: Sometimes what matters most is already there—quietly kept, quietly used, quietly remembered.
draft.title: What Was Already There

draft.author: USP India
draft.body_html:
A grandmother rejects her grandchild’s same-sex partner. Her daughter challenges that rejection, choosing acceptance over judgement.

In Faces from All Races, staged a few years ago, this tension across three generations brought prejudice close to home. Exploring racism, gender bias, body shaming and the struggle to accept difference, the play asked how we respond when someone we love lives differently from what we expected.

We inherit ideas about relationships, behaviour and belonging. Some become so familiar that we rarely question them—until someone close to us gives us reason to look again.

Culture lives in these everyday expectations too. It is passed between generations and shaped by the choices people make.

For the newly established USP, theatre offers a way to explore this lived dimension of culture. Through recognisable characters and situations, it allows us to encounter different perspectives, reconsider familiar assumptions, and open conversations about the lives we share.

seo.description: A theatre reflection on family expectations, prejudice and the possibility of choosing acceptance.

draft.standfirst: Looking back at Faces from All Races, written and directed by Farah Singh.
draft.title: When Acceptance Comes Home

data.body_html:
Urban Suburban Perspectives (USP) works at the intersection of heritage, art and culture. It grew from a shared appreciation of our cultural inheritance, a passion for creative expression, and a desire to translate these interests into meaningful, enduring work.

Our work takes different forms—from heritage conservation and traditional crafts to original theatre. Through these initiatives, we seek to preserve and renew cultural knowledge, nurture artistic expression, and create opportunities for learning, livelihood, and community engagement.

We believe that heritage, art and culture are not merely valuable in themselves; they can also bring people together, foster dialogue, strengthen communities, support local enterprise, and contribute to social, cultural and economic well-being.

Our aim is to develop work that honours the past while engaging with the present and remaining open to new ideas—creating meaningful experiences and lasting value for the people and communities with whom we work.

Every initiative begins with an understanding of the people, places, and traditions involved. This means exploring what already exists, recognising the knowledge and experiences people bring, and considering what new possibilities might emerge.

Bringing together different skills and perspectives creates opportunities for collaboration and experimentation, allowing ideas to develop through participation, practice, and exchange.

We believe there is room for both preservation and imagination. Historic buildings can find new purposes without losing their character, traditional skills can inspire contemporary design, and familiar stories can find new forms of expression.

data.heading: Made by Hand. Shaped by Knowledge.
data.intro: In Rakhigarhi, women are building on existing knowledge and ways of making. Through practice and creative exchange, they are developing skills, individual expression and new pathways to livelihood.

data.body_html:
Ways of choosing materials, judging a form or working with colour are often learned through watching, doing and making alongside others.

USP brings women in Rakhigarhi together with artists, designers and craft practitioners to build on this knowledge. Together, they test and adapt new materials, techniques and ideas, developing work rooted in the place and shaped by the women involved.
data.heading: Not everything we know is formally taught.

data.body_html: Three crafts form the starting point of the initiative. Each brings its own materials, techniques and possibilities for colour, pattern and form.
data.heading: Basket Making. Papier-Mâché. Dhurrie Weaving.

data.body_html: Basket making draws on skills and ways of working already present within the community. Through the initiative, women are exploring new combinations of colour, pattern and form while developing the consistency and finish of the work.
data.heading: Tradition carried forward through colour, pattern and form.

data.body_html: Papier-mâché introduces a different material and process into the initiative. Women are experimenting with form, surface and decoration, developing objects that combine individual expression with the visual language emerging from the group.6
data.heading: A new material. A new direction.

data.body_html: The patterns and motifs woven into the dhurries draw on designs passed down through generations within the community. Women use these as a starting point for new combinations of colour and composition—carrying local textile knowledge into the work being created today.
data.heading: Textile knowledge carried forward through pattern and composition.

data.body_html: The Craft Centre within the Rakhigarhi Haveli and Chaupal will give the initiative a shared home—a place for women to work together, develop designs and techniques, share knowledge and build consistency in what they produce. Visitors will be able to encounter the work and understand the people, materials, and processes behind it.
data.heading: A Place for the Work to Continue.

data.body_html:
As baskets, papier-mâché and dhurries develop into products with wider appeal and economic value, they can create opportunities for women to earn.

Women are also contributing ideas, developing products and becoming more involved in decisions about how the initiative grows.

As the work gains value, so do the opportunities around it.
data.heading: Creating Value Through Craft.

data.aside: Rakhigarhi is known for its extraordinary past. The ambition is to make what is created here part of its future.
data.body_html:
The work begins in Rakhigarhi, with the ambition to reach wider audiences through collections, creative collaborations, and partnerships.

The aim is for craft from Rakhigarhi to be recognised for its quality, character and originality—with women increasingly shaping what is created and where it goes next.
data.heading: From Rakhigarhi, Outwards.

data.intro:
Culture isn’t fixed in time. It is inherited and reinterpreted, questioned and created, lived and shared.

Urban Suburban Perspectives works across Heritage, Art and Culture, exploring how what we inherit continues to find meaning in contemporary life.

data.body_html:
A place, a building, a story, a tradition or a way of making can hold meaning far beyond where it began. USP brings together people, knowledge and different perspectives to explore how these inheritances can remain meaningful in the present—and become a starting point for new ideas, creative expression and opportunity.

Across Heritage, Art and Culture, the work takes different forms, each shaped by its own context and the people involved. Through it, people can develop skills, share knowledge, shape what is created and open new pathways to livelihood.

data.heading:
What We Inherit.
What We Create.
What We Carry Forward.
data.intro:
Culture isn’t fixed in time. It is inherited and reinterpreted, questioned and created, lived and shared.

Urban Suburban Perspectives works across Heritage, Art and Culture, exploring how what we inherit continues to find meaning in contemporary life.

data.body_html:
A place, a building, a story, a tradition or a way of making can hold meaning far beyond where it began. USP brings together people, knowledge and different perspectives to explore how these inheritances can remain meaningful in the present—and become a starting point for new ideas, creative expression and opportunity.

Across Heritage, Art and Culture, the work takes different forms, each shaped by its own context and the people involved. Through it, people can develop skills, share knowledge, shape what is created and open new pathways to livelihood.
data.heading: Heritage, Art and Culture -Kept in Motion.
Shaped by Place, Knowledge and Perspectives.
data.intro: Each initiative begins differently—with a place, an idea, a practice or a question worth exploring. Its direction develops from the context and from the knowledge and perspectives that become part of the work.

data.body_html:

seo.description: USP India's four areas of work: Rakhigarhi, Theatre, Craft & Livelihood, and Workshops & Learning.

data.heading:
5,000 Years of History.
A Place Still Evolving.

data.aside: USP's current work centres on restoring a historic haveli and chaupal and bringing them back into active use. The project explores how these buildings can serve the village today—as places for craft, learning, gathering and welcoming visitors.
data.body_html:
Rakhigarhi is one of the most significant archaeological sites of the Indus Valley Civilisation (IVC), with a history stretching back more than 5,000 years.

It is also a living village—where history, architecture, knowledge, and everyday life continue alongside one another.

Its architecture, materials, and spaces carry traces of generations of domestic life. The restoration seeks to retain that character while adapting the buildings for new uses.

The work itself is also a place of learning. Local construction workers are developing conservation techniques alongside conservation professionals, allowing skills developed through the project to remain within Rakhigarhi. Haveli itself is also a place of learning.

The aim is to demonstrate what is possible—a conserved building that remains recognisable as a home while taking on a quiet new life as a space for community, culture and craft.

What begins with one haveli could grow into a wider pattern of conservation and renewal, encouraging other historic buildings in Rakhigarhi to be restored and brought back into use.
data.heading:
Restoring the Past.
Creating a New Purpose.

data.body_html: The haveli and chaupal have been reimagined as places that can once again be part of everyday life in Rakhigarhi—somewhere to make, gather, learn, welcome visitors and simply spend time.
data.eyebrow: A HAVELI BROUGHT BACK INTO USE

data.body_html: The Rakhigarhi Craft Centre is envisioned as a working space within the haveli, where women make, learn, experiment and develop their work. Basket making, papier-mâché and dhurrie weaving are among the crafts being developed. The Centre will provide a permanent base for working together, exploring designs and techniques, sharing knowledge and presenting what is created.
data.heading: The Craft Centre

data.body_html: For visitors, the haveli and chaupal become a starting point—somewhere to meet people and understand Rakhigarhi's archaeology, history and life today. Through its buildings, craft and stories, visitors connect with the village and the people who call it home. The Heritage Guide Program is part of this experience. Women from Rakhigarhi are developing the knowledge and skills to interpret their heritage for visitors, giving them a greater role in how the village is presented and understood.
data.heading: A Place to Arrive

data.body_html:
Not every part of the haveli and chaupal needs a programme.

There should also be somewhere to sit.

A simple place for chai, cold drinks and conversation gives visitors a reason to pause and gives the haveli some of the informality of a lived-in place.
data.heading: A Place to Pause

data.body_html: Part workshop, part gathering place, part visitor anchor—the aim is for the haveli to feel active and welcoming rather than institutional.

data.body_1_html: The ambition reaches beyond the restoration of a single building. By bringing the haveli and Chaupal back into active use, the hope is to draw people into Rakhigarhi, support local craft and enterprise, and contribute to the village economy.
data.body_2_html: If that activity creates value, other historic havelis may also find new purpose—encouraging further conservation and bringing more of Rakhigarhi's built heritage back into use.
data.body_3_html: What begins with one haveli could grow into a wider pattern of conservation and renewal, shaped by the people who live here.
data.heading:
One Restoration.
A Wider Possibility.

data.heading: Stories Brought to Life. Conversations Opened.
data.intro: Drawn from shared experiences, personal reflections and familiar situations, USP’s productions bring stories to the stage that audiences can recognise, enjoy and sometimes see differently.
data.intro_heading: Original stories rooted in the world around us.

data.body_html:
Culture is not only found in architecture, craft, festivals and traditions. It also lives in family relationships, social conventions, rituals, expectations, and the way people relate to one another.

Theatre allows USP to explore this less tangible side of culture—bringing familiar experiences and situations to the stage through storytelling, humour and performance.

Some stories entertain. Others make us question.
The most memorable can do both.
data.heading: The Worlds We Live In.

data.body_html:
For more than a decade, USP has developed and staged original theatre across a range of subjects, settings and characters.

Each production has its own story, tone, and perspective. Together, they reflect an ongoing interest in the cultural and social worlds around us.
data.heading: More Than a Decade of Original Work.

data.aside_html: Through recognisable characters and situations, the play opens up conversations about money, independence and women’s involvement in decisions affecting their lives.
data.body_html:
The Prayer Meeting Edit is an original comedy set around a chautha—a familiar cultural gathering for prayer and remembrance.

As family and friends come together, relationships, expectations and social conventions begin to surface. What should be solemn becomes revealing, uncomfortable and unexpectedly funny.
data.heading: The Prayer Meeting Edit
data.question:
Beneath the humour lies a question:
how involved are women in the financial decisions that shape their own lives?
data.subheading: A Familiar Setting. A Contemporary Conversation.

data.aside:
The performance ends.
What it opens up can continue.
data.body_html:
The ambition is to continue developing original theatre that is engaging, culturally rooted, and relevant to contemporary life.

As the work grows, USP hopes to reach wider audiences and create space for different stories and perspectives, while remaining connected to the experiences and cultural contexts from which they emerge.
data.heading:
Stories That Travel
Beyond the Stage.

data.heading: Learning, Sharing, and Passing It On.

data.body_html:
For generations, people have learned from one another—through stories told, skills demonstrated, techniques practised and knowledge passed from one person to the next.

USP carries that very human way of learning into its work today—creating opportunities to learn through participation, practice and exchange.
data.heading: What matters is not simply what is taught, but what people are able to do with what they learn.

data.body_html:
Who better to tell the story of a place than the women who call it home?


The Heritage Guide Program works with women from Rakhigarhi to deepen their understanding of the village's archaeology, history and heritage, while developing the skills and confidence to interpret it for visitors.

The program gives women a greater role in how Rakhigarhi is presented and understood, while creating an opportunity for knowledge of their own place to become a livelihood.
data.heading: Knowing Rakhigarhi. Sharing Its Story.

image.caption: The first batch of Rakhigarhi Heritage Guides

data.body_html:
Artists, designers and craft practitioners work alongside women in Rakhigarhi, bringing different skills and perspectives to the making process.

The women’s existing knowledge provides a starting point. Together, they explore materials, techniques, colour, pattern and form—testing and adapting ideas through practice.

Alongside creative development, the aim is to strengthen the quality and appeal of the work, opening up market opportunities and the possibility of better returns for the women who make it.
data.heading: New Ideas. New Directions.

data.body_html:
As the Rakhigarhi haveli and chaupal are restored, local workers learn alongside conservation professionals, gaining practical skills in traditional building techniques.

The restoration becomes a place of learning, with skills that remain with the workers long after the work is complete.
data.heading: Learning Through the Haveli.

data.body_html:
Students can contribute to USP’s initiatives by putting their learning into practice.

One student’s research into Rakhigarhi led to a series of short films created as learning resources for women participating in the Heritage Guide Program. A further Q&A film is being developed around questions visitors may ask.

What began as a student learning project became a resource that others could use.
data.heading: Learning That Becomes a Contribution.

data.aside:
Skills can be used again.
Knowledge can be shared.
Ideas can be adapted and passed on.
data.body_html:
The ambition is for learning to extend beyond any one workshop, project or exchange.

Over time, this can give people greater confidence to participate, contribute to their communities, and pursue new opportunities—including opportunities to earn a livelihood.
data.heading: Knowledge That Continues to Travel.

data.text: USP welcomes students, designers, practitioners and others who want to learn through the work, contribute their knowledge, or share their expertise.
